text: Data Treatment Median lethal concentrations (LC50) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated using the SAS probit procedure. •Survival data were corrected for control mortality using Abbott’s formula5. •LC50 values were calculated in two ways: (1) based on injected MeHg doses, and (2) based on measured THg concentrations; i.e. maternally-deposited THg plus the injected MeHg dose.

•Followed protocol of Heinz et al.4. •120 fresh, unincubated eggs were collected from each species within 24 h of being laid. •Eggs were randomly assigned to 8 dose groups (0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6, 3.2, 6.4 mg g-1 MeHg chloride dissolved in safflower oil) plus a vehicle-control group. •MeHg dose was injected into the air cell and eggs then artificially incubated to pipping (start of hatch). •90% development was the endpoint. •Embryos and egg contents were homogenized, freeze-dried and analyzed for total Hg (THg) by direct mercury analyzer (AMA-254).

The LC50 for murre embryos was 0.48 mg g-1 ww based on MeHg injected into eggs uncorrected for maternally-deposited THg (Fig. 1), and 0.56 mg g-1 ww based on THg measured in the embryos (i.e. maternally- deposited THg plus injected MeHg dose). The LC50 for tern embryos was 0.95 mg g-1 ww based on MeHg injected into eggs uncorrected for maternally-deposited THg (Fig. 2), and 1.10 mg g-1 ww based on THg measured in the embryos. • THg in murre eggs from Coats Island in 2009 averaged 0.16 mg g-1 ww, and for Prince Leopold Island in the high Arctic, 0.40 mg g-1 ww. • THg in arctic tern eggs from Nasaruvaalik Island in 2008 averaged 0.49 mg g-1 ww6. • Compared with LC50 values for 26 tested species2, both thick-billed murres and arctic terns had medium sensitivity to MeHg (0.25 < LC50 < 1 mg g-1 ww) based on injected MeHg. • Based on measured THg, the sensitivity of arctic tern embryos changed to low sensitivity (LC50 ≥ 1 mg g-1 ww).

Introduction •Mercury (Hg) has increased in marine mammals and seabirds (e.g. thick-billed murres) in some regions of the Canadian Arctic over the past few decades1. •Methylmercury (MeHg) is highly embryotoxic making reproduction one of the most sensitive endpoints of Hg toxicity. •Nearly 100% of Hg transferred to eggs is in the form of MeHg. •Significant interspecies differences were found among 26 avian species tested for sensitivity to embryotoxic effects of MeHg2. •Given that Hg is increasing in some Canadian Arctic seabirds, our objective was to determine the relative sensitivities of two Arctic-breeding seabirds, the thick-billed murre and arctic tern, to MeHg exposure.

Given that Hg has been increasing in some Canadian Arctic biota, continued monitoring of these seabird colonies is warranted.
